column4: The section's B002 root ض ح و names exposure to sun; Adam's assurance uses «تَضْحَىٰ» for the heat he will avoid in the Garden. The shared divine promise makes the source's warmth explicitly a boundary of bodily ease.
B003 says «الضحاء» can name «الغداء»; Musa asks for «غَدَاءَنَا» after travel fatigue. This gives the section's forenoon-meal sense a concrete scene of need and provision.
The B004 dictionary branch for ق ل ي describes meat roasted until cooked; Abraham's visitors are served «عِجْلٍ حَنِيذٍ», a direct cooked-meat scene beside the section's lexicon dish.

B004 names a qalya from camel meat and livers; here sacrificial camels become food to eat and share with the contented and needy («وَأَطْعِمُوا الْقَانِعَ وَالْمُعْتَرَّ»), joining the cooked-meat sense to provision.
The section turns the forenoon meal toward hunger; this rite explicitly pairs eating from the livestock offering with feeding «الْبَائِسَ الْفَقِيرَ».
The section's B003 forenoon food stands against want; «إِطْعَامٌ فِي يَوْمٍ ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ» names feeding on a day of hunger, making that contrast concrete.
The hungry-day feeding of 90:14 is for «يَتِيمًا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ»; this ayah identifies the orphan, the person the section says must not be overpowered, as a meal's recipient.
Continuing 90:14's feeding scene, this ayah names «مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ», a second recipient whose destitution sharpens the section's meal-versus-poor-nutrition image.
The section's meal sense meets the Garden assurance «أَلَّا تَجُوعَ»; its own contribution is freedom from hunger, while neighboring 20:119 adds freedom from thirst and sun exposure.
This verse gives food to «مِسْكِينًا وَيَتِيمًا وَأَسِيرًا»; it makes the section's forenoon table a meal shared with the vulnerable, including the orphan named in its prohibition.

The section sets a meal against malnutrition and forbids overpowering an orphan; this verse says unjustly consuming orphans' wealth is «يَأْكُلُونَ فِي بُطُونِهِمْ نَارًا», a specific reversal where food becomes fire.
The section links needy «عَائِلًا» and enrichment with a B004 branch about poor nourishment; here «عَيْلَةٍ» (want) is answered by «يُغْنِكُمُ اللَّهُ», a close root-and-provision parallel.
After the roasted calf in 11:69, the visitors' hands «لَا تَصِلُ إِلَيْهِ»; this ayah adds Abraham's alarm at an untouched meal, a distinct response within the cooked-meat scene.

The section's B003 qahira is milk heated with stones; this Garden description places milk «لَمْ يَتَغَيَّرْ طَعْمُهُ» beside boiling water, marking a boundary between sustaining milk and scorching liquid.
Where 21:68 commands Abraham's burning, «كُونِي بَرْدًا وَسَلَامًا» reverses fire's harm in this ayah; it marks a boundary to the section's qahr image of fire overcoming flesh.
Against the section's meal and cooked-meat lexicon, this passage says the people of the Tree of Zaqqum fill their bellies from it («فَمَالِئُونَ مِنْهَا الْبُطُونَ»), turning eating into torment.
The next ayah completes 37:66's meal with «شَوْبًا مِّنْ حَمِيمٍ»; it makes the hot, harmful accompaniment explicit against the section's nourishing table.
The section's cooking words make food audible; this passage names Zaqqum «طَعَامُ الْأَثِيمِ», the food of the sinner, setting an infernal meal against the shared meal.
Continuing 44:44, the food «يَغْلِي فِي الْبُطُونِ» like molten metal; this is cooking's bodily harm rather than nourishment.
The next ayah sharpens 44:45's boiling comparison with «كَغَلْيِ الْحَمِيمِ», a hot-water image that reverses the section's prepared food.
Where the section evokes cooked food and a morning meal, this passage makes the denied ones eat from Zaqqum («لَآكِلُونَ مِن شَجَرٍ مِّن زَقُّومٍ»), an explicitly punitive food.
This continuation says they fill their bellies from it; the section's meal against poor nutrition becomes its bodily opposite.
The next step is drinking boiling water («مِنَ الْحَمِيمِ») over the Zaqqum, extending the cooked-food scene into a painful drink.
The passage says they drink like thirsty camels («شُرْبَ الْهِيمِ»); this sharpens the contrast with the section's Garden assurance of no thirst in 20:119.
The section's qahr image is fire overpowering flesh; here boiling water melts what is in bellies and skins («مَا فِي بُطُونِهِمْ وَالْجُلُودُ»), a specific bodily reversal.
B002's qahr describes fire acting on meat; here the fire cooks skins («نَضِجَتْ جُلُودُهُمْ») and they are replaced, making the harmful bodily force explicit.
The section's B004 branch names a meat dish; Abraham quietly brings «عِجْلٍ سَمِينٍ» to his guests, a distinct meal scene though this ayah does not say it is roasted.
This continuation of 51:26 says Abraham places the calf before them and invites them to eat («أَلَا تَأْكُلُونَ»), completing the guest-meal scene.
The section's B004 dictionary develops cooked meat as food; this Garden provision includes «لَحْمٍ مِّمَّا يَشْتَهُونَ», putting meat in a scene of desired sustenance, without specifying cooking.
Like the section's meat preparations, this Garden scene offers «لَحْمِ طَيْرٍ مِّمَّا يَشْتَهُونَ»; it supplies a positive food counterpart without claiming the birds are cooked.
The neighboring ayah explains the feeding in 76:8 as for God's face, seeking no reward or thanks; it adds the giver's stance to the shared meal scene.
Allah warns Adam not to be expelled from the Garden or become wretched; neighboring 20:118–119 name hunger and exposure to sun as what the Garden assurance prevents.
The section's table faces poor nutrition; the garden owners secretly bar «مِسْكِينٌ» from their harvest, a concrete withholding of food from the needy.
After 68:24's ban on the needy, the owners go early with firm intent («وَغَدَوْا عَلَىٰ حَرْدٍ قَادِرِينَ»); this adds the planned nature of withholding the harvest.
After their exclusion plan in 68:25, the owners see the ruined orchard and say they must be mistaken; the scene shows the food source itself has disappeared.
After seeing it in 68:26, they say «بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ»; their plan to exclude the poor turns into their own deprivation.
The section joins food and heat; this parable's garden of fruit is struck by a fiery whirlwind («إِعْصَارٌ فِيهِ نَارٌ فَاحْتَرَقَتْ»), showing heat destroying provision.
The section begins with exposure to sun and names B006 plant ash used to wash garments; here garments «تَقِيكُمُ الْحَرَّ» protect people from heat, linking clothing to the same bodily exposure.
The section insists duha is heat as well as light; «الظِّلُّ» and «الْحَرُورُ» are explicitly set apart, making shade and scorching heat the image's climatic boundary.
The section recalls Adam's protection from duha heat; in this Garden scene people see neither sun nor severe cold («لَا يَرَوْنَ فِيهَا شَمْسًا»), extending the protection from exposure.
The section's B006 qily is plant ash used to wash clothes; «وَثِيَابَكَ فَطَهِّرْ» shares the concrete act of cleansing garments, though the ayah gives no ash method.
The section's qahr branch describes fire taking meat; here water like molten metal «يَشْوِي الْوُجُوهَ», a specific reversal from prepared food to scalding harm.
The section's B004 cooked-meat and B002 fire-on-flesh branches meet a different fire scene: the demanded offering is one «تَأْكُلُهُ النَّارُ», a ritual sign rather than a meal.
The people command «حَرِّقُوهُ» against Abraham; this makes fire an act of human harm, the boundary reversed when the next ayah makes it cool and safe.
In a repeated account of Abraham's trial, the people choose killing or burning, but Allah saves him from fire; this adds another specific reversal of fire's overpowering force.
In another telling of Abraham's trial, his people say «فَأَلْقُوهُ فِي الْجَحِيمِ»; this is fire imposed as violence, unlike the section's cooking image.
This neighbor says their plot made them «الْأَسْفَلِينَ»; it completes the attempted burning in 37:97 with the reversal of the burners' power.
The section's B004/B002 fire meanings include cooking and burning; «النَّارَ الَّتِي تُورُونَ» asks about the fire people kindle, a direct human-use counterpart.
This continuation asks who produced the fire's tree («شَجَرَتَهَا»); the section's B006 also names ash from burned plants, connecting fire to plant matter.
This ayah calls that fire «مَتَاعًا لِلْمُقْوِينَ», provision for travelers; it makes the kindled fire useful, a boundary to the section's harmful-fire senses.
The section forbids overpowering the orphan; «لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ» names the opposite failure to honor that same vulnerable person.
The next ayah says they do not urge feeding the poor («طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ»), reversing the section's meal and its care for the orphan.
The section says not to oppress the orphan; «يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ» depicts the opposing act of driving an orphan away.
The next ayah says he does not urge feeding the poor («طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ»), a direct negation of the section's meal-for-need image.
The section sets the forenoon meal against undernourishment; this person «لَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ», refusing to urge food for the poor.
The passage then says there is no food but «غِسْلِينٍ», a painful anti-meal that reverses the section's food as sustenance.
The next ayah says only sinners eat that food («لَا يَأْكُلُهُ إِلَّا الْخَاطِئُونَ»), identifying the opposite eater in 69:36.
The section's meal provision for the needy is reversed by the speakers' confession «لَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ».

The section's B006 qily is ash made by burning plants and used to wash clothes; this verse uses wind-scattered ash («رَمَادٍ») as an image of vanished deeds. The link is only the specific fire-made residue, not a shared cleansing sense.
